data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The preference for better-corroborated theories is defensible on Popper's own terms without smuggling in induction, provided it is framed strictly as a methodological rule for selecting the most informative theory to subject to future falsification, rather than as a prediction of future success or an increase in probability.","counterconditions":[{"case":"The conjecture is refuted if it can be demonstrated that Popper explicitly grounded the preference for corroborated theories in an expectation of their future reliability or truth-likeness (verisimilitude) rather than purely methodological utility.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"The conjecture is refuted if preferring the better-corroborated theory logically entails an inductive inference that the future will resemble the past.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"The conjecture is refuted if the 'methodological rule' defense collapses into a pragmatic wager that implicitly assumes nature is uniform.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"This defense operates by distinguishing between 'corroboration' (a historical report of past performance) and 'verisimilitude' or 'probability' (expectations of future truth). The mechanism relies on the asymmetry of risk: choosing a highly corroborated theory maximizes informational content and exposes the agent to the severest possible tests. If the theory fails, knowledge grows rapidly; if it survives, it remains the best available target for criticism. This choice is rational not because the theory is likely true, but because it offers the highest potential for learning, adhering to the goal of science as error elimination rather than truth accumulation.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
